  wordplay. Consequently, this project's results can enhance the capacity
  of AI to generate humor by incorporating a measure of logical
  consistency, which complements the existing reliance on statistical
  patterns, and ensures that predicted funny words are logically sound.

The model allows for the combination of up to four independently coded signals, enabling greater flexibility in design and improved resistance to interference. We developed an analytical expression to evaluate the signal-to-noise ratio following this coding process and used it to explore various design options. Furthermore, we identified optimal code design problems for specific network configurations and solved some of these numerically. In addition, we provided a framework for evaluating the diversity gains achievable through this coding process. The proposed framework exhibited convergence in various numerical examples, suggesting that the term 'four' in 'four-fold diversity' may be interchangeable with 'the highest attainable diversity gain', thereby eliminating previous interpretations of this term. The term 'fold' refers to an increase by a multiple, as opposed to a precise numerical value. The results obtained with the proposed framework were compared to those achievable through conventional coding methods and were found to be equivalent, indicating that this framework is a suitable tool for eliminating seemingly beneficial but actually non-existent diversity gain induced by coding. navigate unfamiliar spaces without a predetermined map.  To achieve this at a significant speed, a model of the environment must be created through sensory input, which involves detecting and classifying observable features found on its surface. 
  We present a novel method for extracting these surface features from 3D point clouds gathered from the robot's movements. 
  Distinguishing one feature from another is made possible by our model, which enforces a separation based on a set of predefined rules. 
  These rules are determined through the minimal enclosure that includes both the point cloud representing the feature and its local surface. 
  The proximity of the robot's sensor means that a majority of these minima will yield valuable information about the same surface feature, allowing them to be grouped together. 
  By calculating the geometric median of each cluster, a set of distinct surface feature models is created. 
  To validate our method, we used a dataset with manually identified features to compare them to those found by our algorithm, showing a promising degree of overlap. 
  In particular, the dataset in question focuses on the faces of objects that could be useful for grasping, providing a basis for future work on that topic. 
  The code for our method is open-source and available on the GitHub platform. 
  We also created an interactive visualization to manually define and organize surface features for evaluation purposes, which can be useful for various robot tasks beyond grasping. 
  This visualization allows the user to specify features by drawing on the 3D model of the environment and assigns the relevant point clouds to these features based on their proximity. 
  The code for this visualization will be updated to reflect any changes made to the robot's software for capturing surface features. 
  This will in turn affect the validation of any algorithms developed using this visualization, such as those for classifying the features. 
  The classes assigned to the point clouds can be used to guide the robot's movements to obtain more data from the same feature, which could then be combined with the initial data to refine the model of that feature. 
  We plan to apply this validation process to sets of manually defined features to find the common surface patterns across different robots and environments. 
  This will help us determine the general rules that characterize particular features and provide a basis for predicting the existence of certain features based on sensory input gathered from the robot's movements. 
  We also intend to use this validation to develop algorithms for selecting the most relevant features to focus on during the exploration of an environment.

growing interest in using machine learning models for weather forecasting. Nonetheless, achieving significant improvements with existing models for the NLP task of weather forecasting using historical data remains a challenge. To address this issue, we've developed a novel approach that leverages a multi-head self-attention mechanism, coupled with a simple convolutional neural network, for the sequential data of weather forecasts. This proposed model capitalizes on the inherent patterns within time series data, thereby enhancing forecasting accuracy. Furthermore, our model exhibits a clear advantage over a baseline model with a single-head self-attention mechanism. We've conducted a series of experiments with our proposed model using real-world weather forecast datasets and observed a notable enhancement in forecasting effectiveness. To facilitate widespread adoption, our model has a relatively modest parameter footprint. We've made the code and datasets publicly available on reputable repositories for the benefit of the scientific community. The best model achieved a lower MAE of 2.51 and a higher CORR of 0.87 when using the test datasets from the MDA, MET, and TDA datasets at the 48-hour forecast level. The simplest version of our model requires approximately 120,000 parameters to forecast weather conditions with a 48-hour lead time for a spatial resolution of 0.125 degrees x 0.125 degrees. Nonetheless, the total parameter count can be adjusted based on the desired forecasting specifications. The model can be scaled up or down to accommodate various forecasting requirements with a scale-invariant architecture. The evaluation metrics indicate that our model achieves superior forecasting results even when using a limited set of training data. The simplest version of our model can be trained from scratch using a dataset with a temporal resolution of 6 hours for a total of 5 days with approximately 360,000 data samples and 30,000 parameters. Nonetheless, the majority of the parameters are necessary to capture the patterns within the validation and test datasets. We believe that the distinctive architecture of our model, coupled with the inherent patterns in weather forecast data, provide valuable insights into the selection of NLP models for this task. The best model achieved a significant reduction in MAE of 11.5%, 13.5%, and 10% when using the TDA, MET, and MDA datasets at the 24-hour forecast level. Building on the Riemannian metric and dual connection, we establish the theory of quaternionic geodesics and gradient flows. Furthermore, we apply these developments to define the Rayleigh quotient geodesic and gradient flow in the space of quaternionic matrices. Specifically, our results concerning the polar decomposition enable us to tackle decomposition problems as optimization tasks on matrix manifolds. Generally, our quaternionic decomposition theories are applicable to any set of matrices that can be placed into the form $$RZ^T$$, given that $R$ and $Z$ belong to appropriate matrix groups. Notably, our approach provides a unique path to solving certain optimization problems on matrix manifolds by leveraging the properties of quaternions in combination with the Riemannian metric and dual connection. Ultimately, our results regarding the polar decomposition arise from a quaternic application of the Fuglede's theorem to $S_+^2$, offering a solution to a long-standing problem proposed by Roger Brockett. Besides, our approach to defining the polar decomposition via the Rayleigh quotient geodesic flow is a generalization of a method previously introduced by Peter Antonelli for real symmetric matrices. Finally, our findings on the gradient flows of geodesics can be utilized to efficiently compute the polar decomposition of matrices. To that end, we introduce the quaternionic polar decomposition of the map $$R \to RZ^T$$, given a fixed matrix $Z$, which facilitates the application of the gradient flow to matrix manifolds defined by $Z$. Consequently, our results regarding the gradient flows of geodesics become a useful tool in various matrix decomposition problems. By applying a suitable unitary transformation, we derive a new, simplified two-component Bogolubov-de Gennes equation. Next, we analyze the energy spectrum of this model and identify the conditions under which the true ground state emerges, characterized by a non-trivial phase factor. We find that, in contrast to two-component Bose gases, even a small amount of condensate interaction can lead to a phase-fractionated ground state, resulting from the coexistence of components with opposite polarization. Additionally, we demonstrate that in situations where the spinor condensates' interaction is strong enough, the energy spectrum can be explained by a periodic array of barriers within a infinite square well, and as such, we use this model to calculate various physical properties, including phase-fractionation gap, phase-separation threshold, and metastable phase-fractionation phases. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of component density and condensate interaction strength on the energy spectrum and find that our model can be applied to a wide range of component density ratios, but requires a finite anisotropy to manifest the phase-fractionation phenomenon. We also emphasize the experimental significance of this phenomenon by proposing a feasible measurement strategy based on JILA's two-component Bose gas experiment. We conclude that spinor condensates offer unique possibilities for manipulating phase-fractionation phases and might allow for the achievement of phase-fractionation gaps in isolated, single-photon experiments. We stress that our model represents an oversimplified case of multi-spinor condensates and suggest that more complex scenarios, such as doublewell, ring, or quasi-one-dimensional configurations, are worthy of further investigation. We highlight that the term "phase-fractionation" is an umbrella that encompasses both quantum and classical aspects of this phenomenon.   existing annotated datasets and incorporating them into the training data
  for a new model. The assumption behind this method is that the errors
  encountered during the transcription process mirror the complexities of spoken
  language and can be learned from. In support of this assumption, our research
  reveals that the more difficult a spoken sentence is to understand, the more
  transcription errors it will contain. To evaluate the proposed method, we
  compiled a rigorous dataset featuring spoken descriptions of static images and
  found that, when used in conjunction with the corresponding text transcripts,
  it can effectively capture the nuances of spoken language and significantly
  improve the accuracy of ASR systems when tested on unseen data. Furthermore,
  this advantage generalizes to various domains since the proposed method's
  performance on the German dataset German Image Description contains only a
  minimal degree of overfitting when compared to the English dataset English
  Image Description. Moreover, our results indicate that incorporating the
  proposed speech-text alignments into the training data can also yield
  meaningful improvements in the event that the pre-training ASR model has
  already achieved a certain level of accuracy. To ensure widespread accessibility
  of the proposed method, we made the German Image Description dataset
  publicly available. Additionally, the code used to create the speech-text
  alignments has been posted online. The name of this code is Semafor. Semafor

We establish upper limits on the cross-section of Monopole production for various mass ranges, taking into account different spin properties and whether they participate in the strong nuclear force.  For the most unlikely Monopole properties, we set the most stringent limits to date, closing the remaining mass gaps above 800 GeV for non-perturbatively produced, strongly interacting Monopoles.  Furthermore, we narrow the range of possible cross-sections for righthanded WISPs Monopoles, which could be detected in upcoming high-statistics runs at the LHC.  We also examine the potential of future LHC runs to significantly lower the limits on WISPs Monopole masses, either in single-production scenarios or when paired with their antiparticles, for which the LHC has already near-total coverage among masses up to 4 TeV for the most unlikely properties.  Finally, we highlight the complementary reach of the LHC with respect to direct detection experiments for low-mass Monopoles, which could be efficiently searched for using existing low-threshold beam dump or direct detection setups.  We calculate that an order of magnitude increase in beam luminosity at the LHC could reduce the limits on the cross-section of light WISPs Monopoles by a equivalent amount, which we believe could lead to significant breakthroughs in the understanding of dark matter in the future.   Differential Geometry and Topology, where I presented an overview of the recent
  advancements in the study of Gelfand-Krigenmeyer categories. These categories
  were first introduced by the mathematicians Gelfand and Kreigernauer in the
  1950s, building upon the foundation laid by Emmy Noether, Erwin Schrödinger,
  Hermann Weyl, and Eugene Wigner. The notes that follow detail the key
  concepts and modern generalizations of these categories, incorporating the
  incorporation of the principles of geometric invariant theory, moduli spaces,
  and Mumford's geometric invariant theory, as well as the roles that projective
  representations, algebraic groups, and quantum groups play in the study of
  Gelfand-Krigenmeyer categories. The course materials also explore the
  connections to be found between the mathematical framework and the physical
  applications in the study of symmetries in monodromy groups, solving
  quantum field theory, as well as in the analysis of classical and quantum
  perturbation theory. The course concludes by highlighting the fundamental
  questions that remain in the study of Gelfand-Krigenmeyer categories and the
  incentives for continued research in this field. The appendix provides a
  concrete example of the categories that arise from the symmetries of a matrix
  monodromy group, highlighting the presence of both discrete and continuous
  symmetries that result in the categories being neither abelian nor closed.  The

  monodromy groups, the Weyl-Algebraic Branching Rule, the representation

  groups associated with a differential equation. The course materials are further
  supplemented by numerous open questions in the study of monodromy groups.  A
  companion paper, not included in these notes, provides a more in-depth
  exploration of the quantum groups that underlie monodromy groups and the
  differential equations that give rise to these groups. The note also outline

We examine two distinct scenarios: one involving a single traffic network with variable power transmission capabilities along its roads, and a more complex system comprising multiple traffic networks.   effect of improving the existing detectors with additional information and

  beam optimization using simulated data from the current neutrino detectors.

  potential outcomes of beam optimization using simulated data, reinforces the

distinguishing between different quantum
  states that are otherwise indistinguishable. In principle, any two-state system could
  be described using a combination of symmetric and antisymmetric eigenstates, but
  the reality constraint forces the true eigenstates to be approximately symmetric or
  antisymmetric in relation to a defined operation, such as a spin flip. The extent
  to which the ideal arrangement deviates from the true eigenstates is a measure of
  the degree of spontaneous symmetry breaking in that particular quantum state. 
  Consequently, the term "spontaneous symmetry breaking" is more accurately applied 
  to the relationship between the system's Hamiltonian and its quantum states, rather 
  than to the system's Hamiltonian in isolation. A key characteristic of spontaneous 
  symmetry breaking is that the corresponding eigenenergies are split, which has been 
  observed in various physical phenomena, including the Zeeman effect and quantum 
  entanglement, but the term "spontaneous symmetry breaking" is not typically used 
  in these contexts. In contrast, energy splitting is a direct consequence of symmetry 
  breaking in multi-spin systems, such as the Heisenberg model, where the degree 
  of spin entanglement is an indicator of the size of the energy splitting. 
  Interestingly, the energy splitting in these systems can be manipulated through 
  external means, but the physical process of generating energy splitting via symmetry 
  breaking is fundamentally different from the process of quantum tunneling, which 
  involves a direct manipulation of the Hamiltonian rather than the quantum states. 
  As such, the term "spontaneous symmetry breaking" is more appropriately applied 
  to a phenomenon exhibited by multi-spin systems, where the entanglement serves as 
  an indicator of the degree of symmetry breaking, than to the individual spins' 
  Hamiltonian. 
  This understanding of spontaneous symmetry breaking, initially proposed by Powers 
  and Bargmann through their analysis of the adiabatic theorem, has far-reaching 
  implications for understanding complex phenomena, such as quantum entanglement, 
  symmetry breaking, and the Zeeman effect, which are all interconnected 
  concepts. Furthermore, these relationships hold true across various physical systems, 
  including spin systems, electromagnetic transitions in atoms and molecules, 
  electromagnetic transitions in atoms and molecules, as well as Lamb shifts in 
  atoms and molecules, where the energy splitting in these systems is directly 
  related to the degree of spin entanglement.

As a convergence of these technologies, IoVs utilize multiple wireless interfaces to provide safe and efficient connectivity, thereby generating significant interest in interface selection techniques to ensure timely and reliable data transmission. Interface selection in IoVs involves choosing between multiple wireless interfaces to transmit data over the most suitable network, a process that can be optimized using mathematical models and algorithms, but also poses several challenges due to varying delay constraints and network conditions. This research builds upon the framework initially proposed by Le Sueur and Serre for planar systems and expands their findings to a more general setting, allowing us to address systems with multiple degrees of freedom. This characterization, in turn, contributes to the stability analysis of the equilibrium where all oscillators synchronize. This is demonstrated through the Kuramoto model, but the method is applicable to a broader class of systems. A notable connection is established between the geometric properties and the exponential decay of the second moment of the measures representing the system's states. This connection is then used to derive a criterion for the stability of the synchronized state. This criterion is refined through the introduction of a notion we call the measure-theoretic mean curvature, which captures the tendency of the system's configurations to converge to a common state. This measure-theoretic mean curvature is found to be a key factor in the decline of the second moment, thereby influencing the stability of the equilibrium. This is particularly evident in the Kuramoto model, especially when considering systems with coupled clocks. A key advantage of this approach is that it allows us to handle a wide range of systems without the constraint of weak interactions, in contrast to the previous literature. Traditionally, research focuses on analyzing existing protocols, but our work reverses this perspective and uses graph neural networks to construct ideal protocols for information dissemination, thereby reducing the time it takes for agents to obtain critical information.   player chooses between two random options, with associated wins or losses,
  with the possibility of moving to an adjacent space on a grid. The twist
  comes from the possibility of remembering the previous space and moving
  back to it with a certain probability. Our research demonstrates that, no
  matter the randomness of the individual moves, there exists a strategy
  where the overall outcome of the game is always positive, provided the

  size of the remembered portion directly influences the parity of the
  grid's size and has no further effect, while the average outcome of the
  game is determined by the random individual moves and the remembered
  portion's size. Additionally, we discovered specific memory-spaced
  strategies that yield a positive overall outcome even when the individual
  moves are randomly chosen to result in losses. Our findings also extend
  to games where the player can move forward on the grid with a certain
  probability. Furthermore, we found that the most profitable Parrondo game

By assuming the jet's closing angle was less than one degree, our model indicates the jet moved at a speed near the speed of light. By utilizing the light curve data, particularly the initial \gamma-ray pulse's shape, we determined the jet's distance from the source to be approximately 1.6 x 10 to the power of 11 light years. Based on this calculation, the energy released during this initial pulse would be approximately 5 x 10 to the power of 54 ergs, which is a relatively small amount compared to the jet's total energy. Additionally, our model found the opening angle to be approximately 0.4 degrees, the jet's total energy to be approximately 10 to the power of 54 ergs, the radiative efficiency to be approximately 0.04, and the radiation energy to be approximately 4 x 10 to the power of 53 ergs. We also observed that the initial \gamma-ray pulse's spectrum can be described as a conventional Band function, while the late-time \gamma-ray spectrum exhibits an additional high-energy component, often seen in late-stage GRBs, which may be the result of a reverse shock. We were able to determine the time of the reverse shock's onset, which is approximately 7.64 seconds, and the duration of the reverse shock component to be approximately 3.3 seconds. We conclude that GRB 130315A's early phase can be explained by an off-axis relativistic jet, and further research on the spin-down process as well as the reverse shock component is recommended. We also suggest that the off-axis phase may be more common than previously thought, which could provide insights into the physics of GRB jets and the energy sources that power them. However, implementing security measures to protect these exchanges from malicious activity can significantly slow down data transmission speeds, creating a tradeoff between internet exchange efficiency and security effectiveness.  This research introduces three energy-efficient, packet-inspection protocols to effectively balance exchange efficiency and security effectiveness:  The first protocol, Dynamic Packet Filtering (DPF), automatically adjusts data transmission rules based on real-time exchange traffic analysis.  The second protocol, Hierarchical Packet Filtering (HPF), uses a multi-level inspection framework to prioritize the examination of exchange data packets.  The third protocol, Adaptive Packet Filtering (APF), fine-tunes exchange data transmission rules using both real-time traffic analysis and statistical historical data.  We implemented these protocols on a real network testing platform and found that they significantly reduce packet inspection delays while accurately identifying malicious activity.  Furthermore, the data shows that these protocols can efficiently protect internet exchanges from various types of attacks while minimizing packet inspection overhead.  This validates the efficacy of these protocols in providing an efficient and effective security solution for internet exchanges. This could lead to the development of materials that exhibit both high ferromagnetic coupling and unique physical properties resulting from spin-orbit coupling.   highly debated, with both highly luminous Broad Line Region (BLR) and 
  hot jets being capable of explaining their observed spectra. By analyzing the
  correlation between the luminosity of the narrow Line Region (NLR) and the
  luminosity of the 2-10 keV X-ray emission, we investigated the contribution
  of NLR to the X-ray spectra of these sources. Using a detailed radiative 
  transfer model from the NLR, we found that the $L_{X}/L_{[OIII]}$ ratio, 
  which serves as an indicator of the X-ray emission mechanism, varies among 
  different object types. While the ratio is approximately 0.05 for powerful 
  BL Lac objects with high accretion rates, it ranges from 0.001 to 0.1 for 
  X-ray and gamma-ray bright Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars, indicating that the 
  X-ray spectra of these sources are only partially explained by BLR. Moreover, 
  the ratio is significantly lower for quasars with large NLR luminosities, 
  indicating that the X-ray emission in some quasars may be primarily 
  produced by hot jets.  We also found that the ratio is correlated with the 
  luminosity of the X-ray band, which can be understood as a result of the 
  different slopes of the X-ray spectra. However, this correlation may also 
  arise from the varied electron energies in hot jets and their corresponding 
  emission mechanisms.  The $L_{X}/L_{[OIII]}$ ratio is a valuable tool for 
  determining the contribution of NLR to the X-ray spectra of these sources 
  and for identifying the X-ray emission mechanism in different object types. 
  Given its based on observed line ratios, it is independent of the details 
  of the photoelectrical feedback model and is therefore a more direct 
  indicator of the stability of the AGN.  Furthermore, this ratio can be 
  used to estimate the contribution of NLR to the X-ray spectra based on 
  $L_{[OIII]}$, which can be derived from the $L_{[OIII]}$ ratios given 
  in the paper, which are calculated from the luminosities given in the

  leverages the statistical characteristics of aggregate queries and offers a
  flexible trade-off between error rate and sampling size. Furthermore, our
  results illustrate the applicability of COBRA to various types of queries.

  particular query.

  visualize and understand the sampling process in an intuitive manner.

  size for a specific query, an resource that could be utilized in various

Based on a one-dimensional model, we found that even low levels of external pressure can prevent the migration of embedded planets, due to the torque generated by their interaction with surrounding gas. As a result, we found that the migration of embedded planets is more likely in highly pressurized molecular clouds than in their less pressurized counterparts. Neutral particles can be described by a set of transport equations that depend on the collision probability with plasma particles. Colliding with plasma particles determines the fate of neutral particles, whether they are absorbed, move quickly, or react with the plasma. The complexity of these equations means they cannot be solved directly, but rather an approximate method using a closure factor is used to calculate transport. This method was tested on an imaginary tube and compared to a similar study on a simple reactor. It was found that adding plasma particles that neutrals can collide with, especially particles that move quickly, affects transport more than particles that are absorbed. Additionally, the closure factor was found to be influenced by the collision probability, specifically its likelihood and speed, which further influences transport. A key finding in this study is that the closure factor, which is often assumed to be constant across a complex, varies significantly across different areas of the complex and should be calculated individually for each area instead of being assumed constant. 
 
  The neutral particle transport model was applied to a simulation of a tokamak discharge but, due to the model's complexity, had a simulation time that was several times longer than its simplified version. A way to improve this would be to use a different closure method that was successful in another simulation. This other simulation was for a state-of-the-art tokamak with a complex plasma and showed that even with a much simpler model of neutral particle transport, it was still possible to predict the accumulation of neutral particles, which was not expected, and demonstrated that neutrals tend to accumulate in areas with low plasma density and flow speed. 
 
  It was suggested that a more accurate model of the closure factor is necessary to accurately predict turbulent transport but using a simpler model was found to be effective in predicting the accumulation of neutral particles and could be a useful tool for the design of future tokamaks with a complex plasma.

Our research presents the discovery of six new FRBs detected during the survey of the Beowulf radio telescope in Chile, with the addition of three previously reported FRBs from the same dataset.  By calculating the signal-to-noise ratio in multiple time delays, we confirmed the extraterrestrial origin of these events.  With observations from the CHIME telescope, we were able to determine the positions of four FRBs in the sky and narrow down their locations to specific areas.  Analyzing the characteristics of the discovered FRBs revealed that they exhibit pulse widths that are generally consistent with their detection resolutions, along with the presence of scattering in some signals.  Further investigations are necessary to clarify the physical phenomena underlying these events.  The Beowulf telescope's wide frequency range enabled us to gather detailed information about the FRBs, including spectral shapes that varied from single- to multi-component patterns, along with evidence of reburning in some signals.  By combining the delay times from the two telescopes, we established the likelihood of some FRBs occurring in pairs.  The discovered FRBs are considered to be of the pulse-isolated type and are believed to originate from sources with energies within the intermediate range.  By calculating the energies based on their radiated powers and observing frequencies, we found that they fall between the energies of repeated and isolated FRBs.  The extensive data provide a solid foundation for future analyses, including the combination of data from the two telescopes and the investigation of possible pair FRBs.  The discovered FRBs are significant additions to the currently available datasets and contribute to the understanding of intermediate energy FRBs. While these parameters are straightforward for bivariate curves, they are more challenging to define for higher-dimensional surfaces. To address this issue, we introduce new notions of measure and rank, specifically for quintic equations in three variables. These new definitions are chosen to mirror the complexity of linear operators in the polynomial ring, with the measure corresponding to the degree of the operator and the rank reflecting the minimal number of components required to express the function. We then establish bounds on the measure and rank for a particular class of quintic surfaces, which have a specific invariant known as a Falting height. To obtain these bounds, we utilize the relationship between heights and the measures/ranks of surfaces, along with the results from a previous paper that provided upper bounds on the measures/ranks of certain four-dimensional hypersurfaces. The framework introduced here can be applied to other surface categories, such as K3 surfaces and abelian surfaces, with specified embedding properties. The framework also implies that a high-measure quintic surface cannot be globally minimal, which means there exists a quintic surface with a measure greater than a specific constant and whose minimal model has a different measure. The connection between measure and the geometric properties of surfaces is an area that this result helps explore. The bounds on measure/rank are established through the application of height-complexity inequalities, which are general principles derived from the application of effective height inequalities to the measures/ranks of surfaces defined by polynomial equations. These height-complexity inequalities reflect the interplay between geometric properties and computational complexity in the study of polynomial equations. The effective version of one such inequality is proven here, which states that the measure/rank of a surface defined by equations with a specific invariant greater than a constant cannot remain below a different constant, thus providing the desired bounds on measure/rank for such surfaces. The approach introduced here emphasizes the utility of viewing the measures/ranks of surfaces through the lens of height inequalities, which offers a height-complexity framework that can be employed to investigate the relationship between geometric properties and computational complexity for various surface categories. The results on quintic surfaces are further explored in the appendix through the examination of notable examples, along with a discussion on the relationship between measures/ranks and embedding properties of surfaces. The research on height-complexity inequalities is an area that is open to exploration, with potential applications in understanding the connection between geometric properties and computational complexity of surfaces defined by polynomial equations. We propose that the combination of interactions within the climate system, much like those found in systems with spinorial symmetry, leads to a vast array of linear oscillatory modes.  These modes can be understood as the discrete eigenvalues of a linearized version of the climate system's operator, and their associated eigenvectors define the patterns of variability.  Our research indicates that the spectrum of the climate system's operator is comprised of an almost-continuous portion resulting from the intricate interactions between the system's components, as well as a more distinct, discrete portion that reflects the system's symmetries and defines the modes of variability.  To better comprehend the behavior of the global atmosphere, we extracted a reduced representation of the climate system's dynamics, effectively capturing the most fundamental modes of variability and the associated cyclical patterns of high and low pressure.  This understanding was then applied to analyze the patterns of variability seen during different time periods, and our findings suggest that the distribution of the system's energy across these patterns remains relatively stable, while the location and intensity of some patterns have varied significantly over time.  Our research also enables the prediction of the future evolution of these patterns of variability, and such predictions can be tested against data from previous centuries.  In addition, our approach provides a theoretical framework for the origins of the NAO and similar indices of variability.  We believe that a similar multi-scale approach could be valuable for studying the dynamics of other complex systems, facilitating an in-depth understanding of the relationships between the system's components, the spatial patterns of variability, and the associated cyclical phenomena.  To further investigate the applicability of this approach to the climate system, we plan to extend our model to include the effects of changing temperatures on the geometry of the system's operator, as well as the possible breakdown of the system's symmetries and the resulting non-symmetric dynamics.  We propose calling this approach the Spinorial Spectrum, and it could be developed using a combination of observational data and the results of model simulations, providing a unified framework for understanding the dynamics of the global atmosphere and the geometry of the climate system.  We believe that a deeper comprehension of the Spinorial Spectrum could reveal the fundamental reasons behind the stability or instability of various modes of variability, and such understanding could be crucial for making predictions about the future behavior of the climate system.

We have achieved significant insights into optimizing energy and time resolutions, as well as evaluating reconstruction algorithms and physical quantities. These findings demonstrate the potential of the $B$-AIREX experiment to explore a wide range of physics in various energy levels. We highlight the experiment's potential for conducting further research at the BEPCII facility and outline necessary upgrades required to improve its capabilities. We also emphasize the importance of using realistic simulation models in research related to particle physics experiments. We have made the $B$-AIREX simulation toolkit an open-source resource to promote the development of accurate simulation models and to facilitate collaborations among researchers in physics and computer science fields. We believe that sharing this experience and the proposed code could benefit other experiments and help develop more sophisticated simulation models for various applications. We have validated the performance of our proposed simulation pipeline using both theoretical models and real experimental data, and we demonstrate its efficiency on a cloud platform. We also introduce a novel approach using simulation models to train machine learning models on the basis of physical parameters instead of directly using them, and we discuss the benefits of this approach in terms of model scalability, robustness, and the reduction of data mistreatment. We highlight the potential of this approach to develop robust and generalized machine learning models for various applications, and we propose further research on this topic. We also outline our proposed plan to improve the $B$-AIREX detector's capabilities and conduct research on rare processes at the BEPCII facility, and we discuss the necessary upgrades required to achieve this goal. By analyzing the clustering process, we found that heavy gluon clusters possess distinct properties - they are nearly massless, exhibit pronounced long-range attractive forces, and comprise a vast number of quark and gluon monomers. Furthermore, we investigated the behavior of these clusters in multiple contexts: quark gel phase, gluon jet fragmentation, quark jet fragmentation, heavy ion collisions, and QCD de Sitter space. Overall, the hypothesis of heavy gluon clusters offers compelling insights into the physics of quark gel phase, jet fragmentation, and cosmological phase transitions, and may be tested through upcoming experiments at the LHC.   each other can be seen as a self-steering mechanism that influences their

DO) interaction plays a significant role in realizing exotic magnetic phenomena in rare-earth doped perovskites. Understanding the DO interaction is crucial for manipulating these phenomena. The $f$-spin and $p$-spin parts of the DO interaction have distinct spatial distributions, allowing for partial suppression through geometric arrangements of doped ions. A new phenomenon, which we call "magnetic field-induced spin alignment" (MFISA), arises when the magnetic field strength matches the energy difference between the $f$-spin and $p$-spin components of the DO interaction. This leads to a sudden increase in resistivity, an anomalous Hall effect, and other phenomena related to the $f$-spin and $p$-spin interactions. Experimental verification of MFISA is predicted to be feasible through transport and magnetization studies on rare-earth doped perovskites.  The energy scale of MFISA can be adjusted by modifying the perovskite's geometric and chemical environment, offering a scalable approach to induce exotic phenomena in perovskite-based materials.  A theoretical model explaining MFISA provides a basis for understanding and controlling this phenomenon, and potentially, other rare-earth doped perovskite-based materials.  Experimental and theoretical studies demonstrate that perovskite La:CaScO3 is an ideal model system to study DO interaction, and by applying a moderate magnetic field, it can exhibit MFISA at various temperatures, offering a previously unreported energy range for possible studies of perovskite-based materials.  Further research on La:CaScO3 shows that annealing the samples at high temperatures or incorporating more rare earth ions can enhance the percolation of $f$-spin and $p$-spin interactions, leading to more pronounced MFISA phenomena.  The perovskite-based model system offers a robust and scalable approach to induce MFISA phenomena, and potentially, other exotic phenomena related to percolated DO interactions, by carefully selecting the perovskite's geometric and chemical environment through appropriate choice of doped ions and their concentrations, as well as modifying the perovskite's electronic properties by applying pressure or using heterostructures.  The occurrence of MFISA can be diagnosed by transport and magnetization studies, and it is predicted to be feasible to induce percolated DO interactions and MFISA phenomena in perovskite-based materials at various energy scales, which provides a scalable approach to realize exotic phenomena in perovskite-based materials by percolated DO interactions.

Contrary to common assumptions, we discovered that the classical field theory poses a serious threat beyond the inherent difficulties presented by the gluon condensate. In particular, the theory's inherent risks become manifest when trying to extract physical insights from the classical fields' statistical analysis. To tackle this challenge, we developed a novel approach that involves directly quantifying the Yang-Mills theory's inherent risks by re-enacting the classical field configuration's creation through a stochastic reversal process. This approach allows us to assess the impact of the inherent risks on the theory's predictions. This finding is particularly noteworthy as it bears a striking resemblance to the quadratic growth patterns observed in the theory's potential energy landscapes, as previously discovered through Monte Carlo simulations. Our investigations into the stochastic approach also revealed that the inherent risks of the Yang-Mills theory are coupled with the quark backreaction in 1+1 dimensions, with the gluon field's intermediate mass scales exhibiting the most pronounced instability patterns. Our results may be expressed in a more general form that can be applied to all charge densities and can be understood as resulting from the radial expansion's tendency to prioritize the expansion of the most densely packed regions, thus leading to a shift in the initial geometry that manifests as an additional volume scaling in the same way that we observe in our simulations.   from scratch, a challenge that arises during the initial stages of a deep learning
  project when potential architecture designs seem endless. To address this issue, a
  new method called Performance-Diversity Reward Sparsity Branching (PRSB) is proposed,
  which employs reinforcement learning to find a subset of optimal neural network
  architectures based on multiple criteria. The method incorporates a reward function
  that considers both the computational cost of a network and its overall performance,
  and employs an optional diversity encouragement technique to prevent the algorithm
  from converging to a single, superior but limited solution. The proposed PRSB method
  is tested on five widely-used image classification benchmarks using three different
  network types, and the results show that it consistently yields a range of high-performing
  architectures with varying levels of efficiency. The analysis reveals that the method
  excels at exploring a vast design space, even in its earliest stages, and that the
  selected architectures, when trained from scratch, often surpass the performance
  of their corresponding nascent counterparts. The findings suggest that the PRSB method
  is a valuable alternative to the common trial-and-error approach used to determine
  neural network architecture parameters. The proposed framework is an usable benchmark
  and a starting point for further research into efficient neural network design.  The
  code for the Performance-Diversity Reward Sparsity Branching method is publicly available

  has been formally presented in a paper titled "Performance-Diversity Reward Sparsity
  Branching" and published in the conference proceedings of IJCAI 2021.  The paper

We assume that the underlying system dynamics can be broken down into multiple possible states across different time periods, with these states behaving independently. However, the exact period in which the system resides in a particular state remains unknown. To address this uncertainty, we utilize a dynamic programming approach with the aim of maximizing rewards across various time stages. Key challenges arise from the need to take actions based on historical observations and the unknown current system state. To overcome these obstacles, we employ a learning-from-inferences framework that leverages past actions and their resulting outcomes to make more informed decisions about future stages. A key insight gained is that the optimal way to act in one stage is directly tied to the optimal way to act in subsequent stages, with this relationship defined by a set of probability weights that represent the relative importance of each possible action. In contrast to standard MDP solutions, this approach does not involve the use of value functions. Though challenging to solve exactly, we demonstrate that the underlying problem can be framed as a set of linear stochastic control problems over multiple stages, with the condition that each stage's optimal action is a weighted combination of the available actions.   specification of a language's meaning using the same syntax as the
  language itself. This approach enables the precise definition of a
  language's features, including how variables are scoped, functions are
  evaluated, and exceptions are handled, all within a few hundred lines
  of code. By leveraging the familiar structure of the programming
  language itself, surface syntax eliminates the need for the abstract
  syntax trees typically interposed between source code and semantic
  specifications, thereby providing a more direct and manageable way
  to write formal specifications of programming languages. This research
  demonstrates the capabilities of surface syntax by refactoring the
  Wadler's F-framework, a set of functional combinators for describing
  the semantics of programming languages, into a surface syntax
  specification of the F-language itself, and goes on to apply this
  surface syntax to specify the semantics of several programming
  languages, including a surface form that closely mirrors the original
  F-language definitions. Along the way, it becomes clear that surface
  syntax also serves as a reliable, executable interpreter for each
  language, capable of accurately executing valid source code relative
  to the language's own semantics, thus offering a practical use for
  any surface syntax specification. Furthermore, it is shown that
  surface syntax can be seamlessly integrated with existing testing
  infrastructure to automate the execution-based testing of programming

This research focuses on analyzing the propagation of false information in GNNs and investigating potential weaknesses in their design. as an observational tool to explore a neutron star's magnetic field. At first, we develop a code that calculates the interplay between the neutron star's magnetic field and its own rotation, resulting in the Stewart-like electric field, taking into account the effects of general relativity on the geodesic accretion current. This code then helps determine the effects of this accretion current on the Stewart-like electric field, specifically in regards to its impact on the synchrotron emission. We examine the hypothetical scenario of a neutron star with a magnetic field of $10^{10}$ Tesla located in a magnetar-like environment at a distance of $10^6$ meters from the surface, and find that the synchrotron emission would exhibit a consistent pattern, with emission peaking in the X-ray spectrum, even if the star's rotation speed approaches the break-up speed. We also find that the synchrotron emission could be observed in the MeV energy range if the star is spinning quickly enough, thus we believe that further investigation into the dynamics of rapidly rotating magnetars is both necessary and feasible via synchrotron emission analysis. We further analyze the effects of the Stewart-like electric field on the accretion current in relation to the Blandford-Znita mechanism that generates the Stewart-like electric field, and discover that the accretion current is insufficient to explain the strength of the Stewart-like electric field, indicating that the Blandford-Znita mechanism may be more effective than previously thought, especially in rapidly spinning magnetars. We propose that the synchrotron emission from the accretion current could be distinguished from other sources of emission, such as that produced by the star's own spin-powered pulsar radiation, using the unique pattern of emission paired with a particular X-ray spectrum, and suggest that this could be observable with the capabilities of future X-ray telescopes. We also believe that the synchrotron emission from the accretion current could be a major component of the energy outputs of rapidly spinning magnetars, and as such, it deserves further study. We estimate that the energy of this emission could be as much as $10^{39}$ erg/s for the most extreme cases, and propose that this could be achieved with a neutron star spin frequency of approximately 0.4 Hz, and a magnetic field of approximately $10^{11}$ Tesla, and suggest that this could be a key energy output of magnetars in the soft gamma-repeater phase. This technique enables the creation of a 2D five-site array where each site can be selectively addressed, allowing for the manipulation of specific devices while leaving others unactivated. By altering the phase shift values, we demonstrate the execution of both a coherent Jordan-Josephson circuit and a decoherent Josephson junction circuit on the same physical platform. Furthermore, we show the potential to extend this approach to a 2D lattice comprising an arbitrary number of sites, paving the way for more intricate quantum simulations and a potential breakthrough in large-scale quantum computing. In addition to its applicability in quantum computing, this waveguide system also serves as an intricate interferometer, offering a higher order ring resonator design that can be optically emulated using a parametric amplifier as the coupling element, thereby incorporating a nonlinear process into a 2D array via interferometric coupling. This novel strategy could be leveraged to mediate long-range interactions between distant sites, thereby potentially mitigating the challenge of maintaining coherent relationships between widely spaced qubits. This waveguide system operates at a high finesse, enabling low-loss manipulation of light, and as such, it is an efficient design that minimizes photon loss during switching, switching errors are a major obstacle in large-scale quantum processing, and as such, this design could be an invaluable tool in overcoming this challenge. This technique also has implications for utilizing a cavity-based amplifier as an interferometric coupling element for long-range interactions in a 2D array.   complex relationships among species through time, building upon phylogenetic
  analysis. In a PPN, directed edges represent parent-child relationships among
  species, with nodes corresponding to time periods rather than specific
  species. The key feature of a PPN is its ability to exhibit persistence, such
  that for any given time period, the species connected to a particular node
  are exactly those found in that time period. This framework also adheres
  to several other principles to accurately reflect evolutionary history.
  The problem of identifying whether a PPN is valid or not can be solved for
  a finite time frame, but determining whether a PPN is coherent over an
  infinite time span is significantly more complicated. In fact, we prove that
  even a straightforward tree, indicating relationships among species at a
  particular point in time, cannot be accurately reconstructed from a PPN
  for the majority of time spans greater than three, given only the
  information contained within the PPN's root node. Furthermore, we present
  a family of persistent phylogenetic networks that, while valid and
  monophlytic, are incapable of accurately depicting the relationships
  among species at specific time periods. These networks highlight the
  challenges of interpreting persistent phylogenetic networks and the
  importance of considering the passage of time in relation to them.

These theorems state that any such hypersurface can be represented in one of two forms using complex-valued polynomials of m variables, where the number of variables depends on the hypersurface's degree. We also establish that two distinct forms are equivalent to each other and to a specific form with a particular symmetry, and we demonstrate that multiple forms that differ by a complex linear transformation are equivalent. We establish that any polynomial form can be transformed into a normal form using complex linear transformations and that two normal forms are equivalent if and only if their associated symmetries are equivalent. We also develop a fundamental theorem about the symmetries of a polynomial form that is not normal. This research was previously conducted by the noted mathematician Hermann Menger, who did not publish his findings. They are now known as Menger's Theorem. This theorem states that a set of complex linear transformations that preserve the degree of polynomial forms corresponds one-to-one to a set of points in a complex space of a given dimension, for which the number depends on the set's degree. We demonstrate the applicability and relevance of Menger's Theorem to the study of polynomial forms with a given symmetry. Furthermore, if $X$ is a Polish space, then there are exactly three categories of closed sets formed by $2^{\sigma}$-measurable functions: those with measure zero, those that are equivalent to a countable union of compact sets, and those that are homeomorphic to a countable discrete space. This result can be generalized to include sets of functions measured against $M_{\sigma}^{p}(X)$ for any $p\in[1,\infty)$. In the case where $X$ is uncountable, a standard Borel space with a non-trivial Borel measure, then measures $p$ less than 1 will result in spaces consisting of an infinite number of points, while measures $p$ equal to 1 will yield spaces with a countable number of points. The underlying topology of $X$ can be determined from the measure $p$, and thus assigning a topology to $X$ is equivalent to specifying the measure $p$. This topological interpretation provides an alternative explanation for the phenomenon that the topological properties of $X$ are unaffected by measures less than 1. The polisher associated with a Polish space $X$ is defined as the collection of all measures $p$ for which the associated topology is equivalent to $X$, and this polisher is countably tight. The concept of a polisher can be generalized to include tight collections of measures on any topological space. The intersection of a collection of measure algebras that are countably tight will also be countably tight. The collection of measures induced by a set of functions on a space $X$ is not countably tight if $X$ contains an uncountable discrete subset, but the addition of a countable dense discrete subset to $X$ will make the collection countably tight. The relationship between the polish topologies and the polisher associated with a space $X$ is reciprocal, and thus the topological properties of $X$ can be determined from the polisher, and vice versa. The polisher associated with a space $X$ can be viewed as a way to extend the concept of a Borel measure to include measures for any topological property, and this extension is compatible with the standard Borel measures when restricted to the relevant properties.   topology, though this approach has limitations in modern grids with rising
  complexity. This paper presents an automated procedure for achieving relay
  coordination in distribution networks. The proposal utilizes linear and
  non-linear constraints defined by grid theoretical models, ensuring that relay
  operating times conform to a specific ratio in each substation and
  distribution section, even in networks with loop configurations. The
  proposed method first builds a detailed model of the grid, then identifies
  substation and distribution section control areas. It subsequently
  determines proper protection timing for all relays throughout the grid.

  various test networks. The proposed algorithm's computational costs are
  manageable even when analyzing large grids with thousands of buses in a
  matter of seconds. The paper also explores multiple optimization variants
  and presents a concise, automated protection timing standard. The standard
  has already been implemented in several grid projects around the world.  \

  yet their performance falls short when confronted with certain types of inferred data. 
  To address this challenge, we present a novel approach that leverages the contradiction 
  statements in the NLI data to fine-tune the pre-trained language models for specific 
  tasks like inference, paraphrasing, and sentence similarity assessment. 
  The underlying theory suggests that the contradiction statements serve as negation 
  examples that help the model develop a sense of opposition, whereas the premise 
  and hypothesis statements are valuable resources for teaching the model to generate 
  opposing text. 
  To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, we apply it to four diverse datasets 
  covering natural language inference, sentence entailment, paragraph similarity, 
  and sentence paraphrasing. 
  The results indicate that our method successfully harnesses the contradiction statements 
  to improve the models' performance, also revealed through the generated opposing text 
  that meets the standards of quality. 
  In addition, we find that this approach is particularly effective when the data 
  is scarce, as evidenced by our experiments. 
  Additionally, we discover that by utilizing the contradiction statements, the models 
  are able to produce more diverse opposing text, as measured by the similarity 
  scores between the generated pairs.

application in natural language processing (NLP).  The rise of deep learning prompted a shift from statistical methods to neural networks for MT.  Currently, the dominant neural network approach is the transformer encoder, which employs attention mechanisms to focus on specific parts of the input sequence.  However, the limitations of the transformer encoder's computational efficiency and memory usage are significant obstacles in large-scale MT projects.  The challenge we address in this paper is the substantial difficulty of scaling the transformer encoder to large datasets.  To overcome this challenge, we present the novel Masked Span Traversal Transformer (MSTT) model, which replaces the standard attention mechanism with a more efficient Masked Span Traversal attention technique.  The MSTT model reduces computational costs and requires less memory than the traditional transformer encoder by eliminating the need for the cached attention weights.  Furthermore, we derive a faster sampling method to obtain multiple future mask spans from a single forward pass, resulting in a significant improvement in our experiments compared to the baseline.  The results show that our MSTT model achieves superior performance compared to the baseline transformer encoder in various NLP tasks, including language modeling and machine translation.   implementation of SwitchPocket, including its key components and how
  it protects against common FTP attack scenarios. Furthermore, we present
  the results of our testing and performance evaluation of SwitchPocket.

  our results demonstrate that SwitchPocket can process thousands of
  forwarding table entries per second, supporting large SDN deployments.

The unique combination of variables that characterizes a crystal structure makes it distinct from the more straightforwardly invertible phenomena of parity and time-reversal symmetry. Generally, inversion-symmetric point groups are composed of 32 possible group classifications, taking into account the spatial arrangements of atoms within the lattice. This study delves into the specifics of these inversion-symmetric point groups, detailing their categorized crystallographic classifications and the associated symmetry operations that define each. Inversion-symmetric point groups can be categorized across three main dimensions: those with centrosymmetry at the unit cell level, those with centrosymmetry localized to specific atomic sites, and those without any centrosymmetry – the latter being more complex and encompassing all 32 possible classifications. A key aspect of this discussion involves the distinction between wavevectors that represent inversion-symmetric phenomena versus those that are inversely symmetric. The former, which correspond to wavevectors located at the midpoint of Brillouin zone boundaries, are more relevant to the phenomena in question. The study also explores the relationship between these inversion-symmetric point groups and the associated phonon anomaly phenomena observed in Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$NbO$_3$ dioxide compounds. The inversion-symmetric point groups can be further understood through the more general concept of the little group, which defines the symmetry of a phenomenon within a crystal structure and determines the specific atomic vibrations that exhibit inversion-symmetric phenomena. The little group for these phenomena is characterized by the $A_{2g}$ irreducible representation of the $O_h$ point group and the $B_{2g}$ irreducible representation of the $D_{4h}$ point group, and is responsible for the coupling between the dipolar strains and the atomic vibrations within these compounds. The little group's associated phonon anomaly phenomena are represented by a specific wavevector located at ($\frac{1}{2}$, 0, $\frac{1}{2}$)) within the hexagonal Brillouin zone. The inversion-symmetric point groups and the associated little group definitions both emphasize the importance of viewing crystallographic classifications from the perspective of inversion symmetry, especially when evaluating the phenomena of phonon anomaly in dioxide compounds. The related research questions, methodologies, and key findings from Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$NbO$_3$ dioxide compounds provide a concrete example of how inversion-symmetric phenomena are observed and can be described using the tools of group theory and wavevector representations.

the first exoplanet, the primary challenge remained finding planets similar to Earth.  As observatories advanced and new techniques became available, the focus shifted towards detecting mini-Neptunes and super-Earths.  While these planets are of interest for studying gas giant planet formation, they are not suitable for evaluating Earth-like planet formation models.  To address this limitation, we introduced the "Migration Limit Theory", which predicts that the most abundant planets should have masses between 5-25 times that of Earth, likely resulting from giant planet migration influencing their orbital paths.  To test this hypothesis, we developed CONCEPT, a comprehensive planetary population model that simulates the effects of giant planet migration on planetary architectures.  By applying CONCEPT to existing exoplanet surveys, we identified a population of previously unreported planets likely formed through Earth-like planet formation processes, which could be discovered by future telescopes with a magnitude limit of 13-14.  We also predict that the next generation of telescopes with a magnitude limit of 12-13 will be able to find the most abundant type of planet, which we call "Mid-Earths", with characteristics that include orbital paths between 0.5-1.5 astronomical units from their stars and with surfaces capable of supporting liquid water.  To highlight the significance of discovering these planets for understanding gas giant planet migration and formation, we propose the term "Planetary Shearing" to describe the process that leads these planets and predict that about 30% of Mid-Earths will result from "Planetary Shearing" which could also be responsible for the formation of mini-Neptunes and super-Earths.  By focusing on these previously unreported Mid-Earth planets, we believe we can gain a deeper understanding of gas giant planet migration and formation and also find the key to evaluating Earth-like planet formation models.  To achieve this, we propose a new priority list for future telescope missions that prioritize the discovery of these Mid-Earth planets in the 5-25 Earth mass range, which we call TESS-30, with the potential to greatly advance our knowledge of planetary formation and also support future direct imaging missions that look for habitable planets.  By working together, we believe we can get closer to finding life outside of our solar system.  To facilitate this, we propose a collaborative framework that includes joint data analysis, research priorities, and mission development with the goal of delivering a comprehensive and coherent plan for searching for the most abundant type of planets that could support life

  The Yang-Mills heat flow and the Einstein heat flow are both parabolic systems of
  partial differential equations with heat flow characteristics. The strong energy

  heat flow, even with smooth initial conditions, can produce solutions that are not
  smooth, demonstrating that these systems can exhibit a decay in solution
  smoothness. This contrast to the expectations based on general principles, which
  suggest that a parabolic system like these would maintain solution smoothness in
  the absence of a singular source. A key result to be presented is a recent
  sharpening of an earlier estimate, which implies that these systems create a
  singular source with a particular magnitude, offering a more precise match to
  known solutions formed through other means, such as the formation of an
  asymptotically de Sitter universe in an Einstein-Einstein-Minkowski system.  A
  key feature of these examples is that they involve a universal singular source
  formation, which could be viewed as a type of universal closure, that these
  systems apply to themselves, as opposed to an arbitrary system of parabolic PDE.

  investigated the accuracy of our sensor reliability indicator among different

self-doped, with minimal resistance at very low temperatures, and that these film 
properties remain stable even when the substrate is changed from Si to Al2O3.

behavior may be more feasible with Nb-doped SrTiN than with Nb-doped SrTiO3. 
To that end, we propose that Nb-doped SrTiN provides a promising and accessible 
platform for realizing self-doped states and related phenomena.

magnetized plasma can be explained 
  by the turbulent electromagnetic fields, using an extension of the kinetic cross-field model.
  By integrating the full electron drift-averaged equation, we account for the influence 
  of turbulent magnetic fields on electron behavior. As a result, we find that the 
  transport velocity remains resistant to an increase in the strength of magnetic fields, 
  and we determine that the transport velocity is, in fact, determined by the 
  fluctuating magnetic field strength, which can be accurately measured on the Earth, 
  and potentially explains the similar transport rates observed on the Earth and Mars. 
  Furthermore, our model implies that transport velocities are susceptible to enhancements 
  through the stimulation of strong electrostatic fluctuations within the plasma and 
  suggests that plasma transport could be greatly affected by phenomena generating 
  strong electrostatic fluctuations, such as solar wind interaction with the planet. 
  We also find that the model can be simplified to align with previous models 
  presented in literature. 
  Our extended kinetic cross-field model reveals that the distribution of electrons 
  remains anisotropic, with a reduced distribution within the plane perpendicular 
  to the magnetic fields compared to the plane parallel to the magnetic fields, 
  and we find that the model can be further explained by the interaction of 
  electrons with the turbulent magnetic fields through the curvature of the electron 
  orbit rather than through the gradient of the electron distribution. 
  We validate our model through comparison with Monte Carlo simulations and 
  a global MHD model of the Mars atmosphere. 
  Our findings provide a clear, physically-defined explanation for the phenomenon 
  of cross-field transport in the plasma environments of the Earth and Mars. 
  We also identify the key processes influencing cross-field transport in the plasma. 
  We propose that the extended kinetic cross-field model can be applied to various 
  planetary settings with the presence of strong magnetic fields, such as gas giant 
  atmospheres and dusty plasma environments. 
  Our model highlights the critical role that turbulent magnetic fields play in 
  shaping the anisotropic electron distribution, which in turn determines the 
  transport velocity in the plasma. 
  We believe that the model provides a valuable, physically-based framework for 
  understanding and analyzing the transport processes within the plasma environments. 
  We also suggest that the model can be utilized in various numerical simulations 
  of the plasma environments with the presence of strong magnetic fields, such as 
  atmospheric escape simulations of the Mars atmosphere.

By adjusting the magnetization of the accretion disk, we can determine the appropriate non-relativistic reconnection scenario to employ in our calculations. Our model successfully replicates a wide range of observations and provides new insights into the source of gamma-ray radiation in these systems. This research focuses on examining the various prediction learning techniques of agents in a simple decision-making model. The study investigates how agents, using prediction learning methods such as full, partial, and no information about other agents's actions, attempt to control a dynamic system to achieve a specific objective. The analysis into different information sets reveals the risks and benefits of using system feedback for predicting other agents' actions. Furthermore, the study explores the implications for safe and optimal control when learning predictions from past system data. The analysis demonstrates how the accuracy of predicted actions affects control performance and highlights the limitational aspects of using historical system data. The research also analyzes a key scenario where the system follows a linear pattern and provides a nonlinear control policy. The theoretical findings are validated through a numerical example involving the control of a random walk system. The results indicate that the efficacy of prediction learning techniques is system-dependent and emphasize the importance of automating safe and optimal control policies based on real-time system feedback, if possible. The study suggests that before applying automated control policies, it is crucial to assess the underlying system dynamics and consider the implications of using historical data in relation to the system's memory and learning patterns. The research implies that both agents with curved and linear learning patterns can be effectively controlled but highlights the challenges in controlling systems with curved learning patterns by agents with no inherent memory. The paper also discusses potential approaches to developing such control policies and highlights the critical role of providing accurate feedback in relation to the actions taken by the agents. The study emphasizes that the development of control policies for predictive agents is a promising area for future research. The research on the random walk system and the comparison between using full, partial, and no information about future system states through the second-order autocorrelation provide a theoretical framework for understanding the implications of different prediction learning strategies on complex system control. The study implies that the capacity to control complex systems successfully is closely tied to the predictive learning abilities of the agents involved and suggests that safe and optimal control policies for predictive agents are crucial technologies for successfully controlling complex, dynamic, multi-agent systems. The research highlights the need for further investigation into how to develop and validate control policies for predictive agents in relation to specific system dynamics and emphasize the importance of testing control policies thoroughly across different system scenarios. The paper also suggest that the analysis of the random walk system and the comparison between using full, partial, and no system information can be extended to a wider class of linear systems and the corresponding control policies have been proven to be efficient

Additionally, we derive an approximate upper bound on the (epsilon, delta)-DP XNN model's risk, utilizing the algorithm's secondary complexity measure and its relationship to the XNN training data. This analysis facilitates a quantitative assessment of the trade-off between the desired level of data privacy and the desired model accuracy. We validate the efficacy of this approach in maintaining a suitable balance between data privacy and model performance by conducting a series of experiments on various XNNs, using both synthetic and real-world data. These experiments reveal that this approach can yield a significant improvement when there is a large gap between the initially chosen epsilon value and the minimum required value, in comparison to directly using a smaller epsilon value. This finding underscores the importance of determining the minimal epsilon value necessary to meet the required data privacy standards, rather than arbitrarily selecting a small epsilon value in an attempt to balance data privacy and model performance. We also find that this approach can be further enhanced by employing a progressive decrease in epsilon values during the training process, using the intermediate models to facilitate this reduction, and that this method is robust to various XNN architectures and dataset characteristics. However, this approach does impose a significant computational cost on the training process, exceeding the cost of training an non-differentially private XNN by a factor of (1/delta). We address this issue by introducing a theoretically grounded strategy for reducing the computational cost of this method, and validate its efficacy on a dataset with characteristics that are amenable to efficient risk minimization while ensuring (epsilon, delta)-DP, albeit this dataset is too large for this method, and propose future work on determining the theoretical parameters for applying this method to such datasets. We also make our implementation publicly available in the hope that it can be utilized by the community in evaluating the efficacy of this method on larger datasets. Our findings reveal that even high-performance models struggle when faced with choosing the correct option from a set of misleading alternatives, highlighting the significance of developing strategies to tackle this problem. Our approach utilizes a specialized model that can rule out incorrect options before selecting the correct one, and our results indicate that this methodology yields substantial improvements over using random choice methods to select the correct option. Our research also implies that, at the current stage, incorporating more context is not always beneficial, and there are situations where limiting the context leads to greater performance gains. Our framework provides a foundation for addressing the challenges posed by multiple-choice QA scenarios, and our code is available for use at https://github.com/ghrua/mcc.   requires correlating images. The process is crucial for various high-level 
  applications, including stereo reconstruction, motion estimation, and object 
  recognition. Nonetheless, achieving accurate matching between densely populated 
  images is extremely challenging. The issue is further compounded when analyzing 
  dense matching across different image types, including grayscale and binary. 
  Grayscale matching involves determining the maximum correlation, while binary 
  matching requires identifying the largest zero-crossing in the image's 
  second-derivative. Our proposed algorithm, called the Decoupled Extended 
  Zero-Crossing Point (DXZCP), first locates an initial estimate for zero- 
  crossing points in binary matching, and then employs these points to guide 
  an iterative process that yields the maximum correlation in grayscale matching. 
  The resulting algorithm exhibits superior performance compared to the 
  traditionally preferred Zero-Crossing Point (ZCP) method.

  publicly available at https://github.com/ymj0925/DXZCP.

  online, such as clicking on web pages. Since web data is often poorly formatted, 
  it's crucial to assess its suitability for use in machine learning. We propose a 
  simple, efficient method to gauge the quality of web data for NLP, relying on 
  a minimal set of easily identifiable features. This approach was effective in 
  distinguishing between effectively and inadequately labeled data, as determined 
  by its performance in supervised learning tasks. We discovered that a tiny 
  percentage of web data (approximately 0.1%) is both readily accessible and 
  of high quality. This discovery suggests that active learning may not always 
  yield substantial gains in performance, given the existing gap in quality 
  among web data. We found that a significant improvement in performance can be 
  achieved by incorporating a small amount of high-quality web data into our

  our approach outperforms them in detection accuracy. Our framework has the added 
  benefit of being easily adaptable to multiple data types and sources. To that

  learning-based attacks on text datasets, which we're making publicly available for

  array of optical detectors aimed at detecting air showers resulting from

  record the footprints of these events, Mageac can identify the direction
  and energy of the cosmic rays that caused them. This paper outlines the

  maximum likelihood method to first estimate the efficiency of detecting events
